scenarios.scenario_description: A scenario involves a black ball at 20°C and a shiny ball at 40°C in a room. Students are asked which emits thermal radiation at the greatest rate.
scenarios.key_insight: While a dull (black) surface has a higher emissivity ($\epsilon$) than a shiny one, the rate of radiation is proportional to $T^4$. The temperature dependence dominates. $1 	imes (313)^4 > 0.1 	imes (293)^4$. The hotter, shiny object radiates more total power.
discrimination_factors: Identifying the Stefan-Boltzmann law dependence on Temperature
Resisting the heuristic 'Black = Good Emitter' when surface property is secondary to temperature

scenarios.scenario_description: A beaker of water at 25°C has ice added to it. Students must determine the final temperature or state of the mixture.
scenarios.key_insight: The energy required to melt ice ($L_f$) is distinct from the energy required to change temperature ($mc\Delta T$). Students must check if the energy available from the warm water is sufficient to melt all the ice before calculating a temperature rise. If the ice fully melts, the final $T$ is found by calorimetry; if not, the final $T$ is 0°C.
discrimination_factors: Setting up the inequality $m_{water}c\Delta T > m_{ice}L_f$

scenarios.scenario_description: A star expands (radius increases by 100x) and cools (surface temperature halves). Students calculate the new total power radiated.
scenarios.key_insight: This tests the manipulation of compound proportionalities in $P = k R^2 T^4$. Students must calculate the combined effect: $(100^2) 	imes (0.5^4) = 10000 	imes 0.0625$. Many students will linearize one or both variables.
discrimination_factors: Handling large integer powers and roots (4th powers)

scenarios.scenario_description: A system of two copper bars in series (or a composite wall) has different temperatures at the boundaries. Students are asked to identify the correct Temperature vs. Distance graph.
scenarios.key_insight: In steady state, the rate of heat flow $dQ/dt$ is constant through the materials. For materials of equal thickness, the temperature gradient $\Delta T / x$ depends on thermal conductivity. A steeper gradient is required for the insulator. The graph must show a 'kink' (change in slope), not a straight line.
discrimination_factors: Understanding the relationship between conductivity and slope in thermal equilibrium graphs

scenarios.scenario_description: An electrical heater warms a metal block in air. The temperature rises by a known amount in a known time. Students are asked to find the energy lost to the surroundings.
scenarios.key_insight: Energy supplied ($P 	imes t$) is partitioned into energy stored ($mc\Delta T$) and energy lost. Students cannot simply use $mc\Delta T$ or $Pt$. They must find the difference: $E_{lost} = E_{in} - E_{stored}$.
discrimination_factors: Applying conservation of energy to open systems
Avoiding the 'obvious' answer that represents only total input energy
